header:
2 people invest **$10,000**
in January 2000. Who wins?

verdict.text:
Behind for 14 years.
Then **≈ 2.7×** Sam's money.

notes: Alex: $10,000 in an S&P 500 index fund on 1 Jan 2000, dividends reinvested, no fees or tax, compounded with the index's calendar-year total returns: 2000 −9.10%, 2001 −11.89%, 2002 −22.10%, 2003 +28.68%, 2004 +10.88%, 2005 +4.91%, 2006 +15.79%, 2007 +5.49%, 2008 −37.00%, 2009 +26.46%, 2010 +15.06%, 2011 +2.11%, 2012 +16.00%, 2013 +32.39%, 2014 +13.69%, 2015 +1.38%, 2016 +11.96%, 2017 +21.83%, 2018 −4.38%, 2019 +31.49%, 2020 +18.40%, 2021 +28.71%, 2022 −18.11%, 2023 +26.29%, 2024 +25.02%, 2025 +17.88%. Year-end values: 2002 $6,239; 2007 $11,407; 2008 $7,187 (= $11,407 × 0.63, the −37% row); 2013 $16,398; 2014 $18,643; 2019 $32,413; 2025 $75,285, shown to the nearest $100 with ≈. Sam: $10,000 × 1.04^n, a hypothetical steady 4% a year (his stated plan), n = years since Jan 2000: 2002 $11,249; 2007 $13,686; 2008 $14,233; 2013 $17,317; 2014 $18,009; 2019 $21,911; 2025 $27,725. Sam leads at every year-end 2000-2013 (14 year-ends); Alex leads from 2014 ($18,643 vs $18,009). Final ratio $75,285 ÷ $27,725 = 2.715 ≈ 2.7×. Growth multiples on the $10,000 stake (lookOpts.summary): Alex $75,285 ÷ $10,000 = 7.53 ≈ 7.5×; Sam $27,725 ÷ $10,000 = 2.77 ≈ 2.8×. 2000-2002 cumulative: −37.6% (Alex down to ≈ $6,200). Same data as the clean-sheet, live-sheet and becker-rig samples, so the looks compare like for like. Captions on, a start row at 0 s (frame 1: both panels landed on the stake), a crash row, a lead change that lands with its event (only Alex's panel flashes), a summary line, the full table at 12.8 s (8 rows in a room for 6 at 44 px: the two plainest rows, 2013 and 2019, give way; Start, the 2008 crash and the 2014 lead change stay), a hard-cut winner flood at the two-line verdict.
